rationale: B wins because it marks the weak beams before the founder walks on them. Its line, "No new apparel line announced is not the same as 'no new apparel line,'" is exactly the kind of guardrail this update needs. A has real angles, but it keeps dressing guesses as facts, especially "something no major apparel brand has attempted" and "no publicly traded apparel company could defend to shareholders."
gaps_in_A: "something no major apparel brand has attempted" is an unsupported comparative claim. The update says 70+ stores and mail-in repairs, not category leadership versus every major apparel brand.
"Patagonia's free-repair bet is designed to shorten its own sales pipeline" states motive and commercial effect the facts do not prove. That is a thesis, not a known fact.

"no publicly traded apparel company could defend to shareholders" imports a sweeping capital-markets argument without evidence. It may be true enough for a columnist after reporting; it is not pitch copy yet.
"four viable journalist shapes exist" is too breezy. The data and counterposition angles are blocked until Patagonia supplies timeframe, economics, or an executive willing to own the tension.
gaps_in_B: "repair counter in every US store" invents a physical counter and store-floor function. The facts only support drop-off at 70+ stores and mail-in repairs.
"Patagonia's newest store rollout has nothing new to sell" overstates the supplied fact. "No new apparel line announced" does not mean Patagonia has nothing new to sell.
"Story type: trend" is the wrong label for the first angle. One company rollout is not a trend unless you bring external evidence, which this set correctly says it does not have.
"That reporter will write the story with or without your cooperation" is useful pressure, but a touch theatrical. The stronger move is the proof list that follows, not the chest-thump.
